scope: Bounded evidence review for small, solvent-free home prototypes: purchased PCL remolding and an aqueous alginate/wax comparator. No experiment has measured waterproofness, compostability, toxicity, mechanical performance or novelty.
redistribution: Only citation metadata, short paraphrased factual subsets and retrieval fingerprints are committed. Source articles, manufacturer PDFs, photographs and full page captures are not redistributed.
evidence_rules: Keep verified primary measurements, review explanations, publisher-abstract facts and manufacturer claims separate.
Water insolubility, contact angle, water-vapor permeability, swelling, leak resistance and continuous-immersion durability are different endpoints.
Mass loss and fragmentation are not proof of complete microbial conversion to carbon dioxide, water and biomass.
Certification scope belongs to the tested grade, formulation and article geometry; it is not inherited by a new blend.
Native starch is not thermoplastic starch; a published high-shear/high-temperature blend method does not validate low-temperature hand mixing.
search_limits: Scoped searches through Crossref and Europe PMC and direct source retrieval. Not an exhaustive literature, patent, certificate or exact-recipe novelty review. No verified primary home-compost mineralization assay for the specific craft grade or proposed 5/10 wt% native-starch blends was found.

sources.title: InstaMorph Moldable Plastic: Material Safety Data Sheet, Version 2
sources.evidence_level: manufacturer product information; not independent performance validation
verified_factual_subset: Reviewed internally on 2015-06-22; the 2022 upload filename is not an updated internal review date.
Section 3 identifies greater than 99% 2-oxepanone homopolymer, CAS 24980-41-4 (polycaprolactone).
Section 9 lists a melting range of 58–60 degrees Celsius and insolubility in water.
Section 2 says not classified according to GHS; sections 4 and 8 still address hot-product contact and eye protection.
Sections 9–10 place decomposition at approximately 200 degrees Celsius; this is not a recommended processing temperature.
Section 12 gives no persistence/degradability information while also asserting readily biodegradable without a test method or result.
transfer_limits: Water insolubility does not establish a pore-free or leak-free home-molded article.
Not GHS classified does not mean hot water or softened polymer cannot burn.
The ecological assertion is not independent biodegradation data, a home-compost certificate, or evidence for an arbitrary filled article.
Do not transfer product claims to pigments, fillers, other suppliers or applications without their own evidence.

sources.title: InstaMorph: How to use InstaMorph instruction image
sources.evidence_level: manufacturer product information; not independent performance validation
verified_factual_subset: Instruction graphic specifies heating water to approximately 150 degrees Fahrenheit / 66 degrees Celsius.
Add pellets, wait approximately two minutes until clear, remove using a tool, and mold.
transfer_limits: This is vendor processing guidance for its unfilled product, not an experimentally validated recipe for native-starch blends.
Two minutes is the depicted vendor guidance, not proof that every specimen thickness or quantity reaches a uniform temperature.
Use tools to remove material and allow comfortable cooling before handling; avoid trapped hot water.

sources.title: InstaMorph frequently asked questions
sources.evidence_level: manufacturer product information; not independent performance validation
verified_factual_subset: The vendor says the material has not been formally certified as food safe by the FDA.
The vendor says it is not dishwasher safe because water above 140 degrees Fahrenheit can soften it.
The vendor describes pressing the softened material into molds rather than pouring it.
The vendor gives watertight perfume bottles and flower vases as possible uses.
transfer_limits: The watertight-container statement is a vendor example, with no retrieved leak-test method, specimen dimensions or measured result.
No food-contact, potable-water or medical claim is established by the craft product information.
Do not use the FAQ room-temperature density of 1.55 g/cm3 as a generic PCL input; it was not independently resolved.

sources.title: Plastimake: How to use Plastimake
sources.evidence_level: manufacturer product information; not independent performance validation
verified_factual_subset: The manufacturer describes hot-water softening at about 60 degrees Celsius.
It instructs users to wait until comfortable to touch before shaping and warns that pockets of hot water may remain.
It recommends keeping the finished item away from heat.
transfer_limits: Instructions for a different craft product are supporting handling context, not a grade-equivalent specification for InstaMorph.
The page recommends boiling water, but the selected experiment instead follows the lower-temperature InstaMorph guidance with measured water temperature.

sources.title: Sustainable Cotton Gin Waste/Polycaprolactone Bio-Plastic with Adjustable Biodegradation Rate: Scale-Up Production through Compression Moulding
verified_factual_subset: PCL grade Capa 6800 (reported molecular weight 80000) was compared with cotton-gin-trash/PCL and cotton-gin-trash/PEG/PCL composites.
Composite extrusion used zones 88–101 degrees Celsius and a reported melt temperature of 105 degrees Celsius; pressing used 80–105 degrees Celsius and 6.3 tonne force.
One-centimeter-square film pieces were buried in premium potting mix at 30 degrees Celsius for two months, with periodic watering and triplicate specimens.
The reported pure-PCL weight loss was approximately 4% after one month and 16% after two months; the 40% cotton-gin-trash / 60% PCL film reached approximately 100% weight loss after two months.
transfer_limits: Soil specimen mass loss and disappearance are not a carbon-dioxide mineralization balance, ecotoxicity assessment or home-compost certification.
Controlled 30-degree-Celsius soil and thin films do not establish the fate or timescale of a thick household part or an arbitrary compost heap.
Cotton-gin-trash composites are not native-starch composites. Their dry powder preparation, extrusion, and forceful pressing are not reproduced by low-temperature hand kneading.
No recipe-specific room-temperature leak or long-immersion result transfers to the present home prototypes.

sources.title: Biodegradable Thermoplastic Starch/Polycaprolactone Blends with Co-Continuous Morphology Suitable for Local Release of Antibiotics
verified_factual_subset: The composition grid includes TPS/PCL mass ratios 10/90 and 20/80 as well as other ratios.
TPS was made from 70 wt% wheat starch / 30 wt% glycerol with six parts water per part starch; gelatinization was at 65–75 degrees Celsius and drying at 25 degrees Celsius for three days.
TPS and PCL were subsequently mixed at 120 degrees Celsius, 60 rpm for eight minutes and pressed at 130 degrees Celsius under 50–100 kN.
transfer_limits: TPS is pre-gelatinized and glycerol-plasticized starch, not dry native cornstarch.
This is evidence for established PCL/starch blend prior art and processing complexity, not evidence that 5% or 10% native starch can be homogeneously dispersed by hand at 66 degrees Celsius.
The biomedical target and material processing do not establish household food-contact safety, waterproofness, or environmental mineralization.

sources.title: Biodegradation of Polycaprolactone Powders Proposed as Reference Test Materials for International Standard of Biodegradation Evaluation Method
sources.journal: Journal of Polymers and the Environment
sources.evidence_level: primary research; publisher abstract only; full article not retrieved
verified_factual_subset: The publisher abstract reports PCL powders tested in aqueous medium at 25 degrees Celsius by ISO 14851 oxygen-demand methods.
It also reports controlled-compost tests at 58 degrees Celsius by ISO 14855-1 and ISO/DIS 14855-2 carbon-dioxide methods.
Powder particle classes included 0–125, 125–250, 0–250 and 250–500 micrometers; the abstract reports reproducible biodegradation.
transfer_limits: The 58-degree-Celsius controlled-compost test is not a home-compost test.
Powders have much higher specific surface area than thick household objects.
No numerical conversion percentage or duration is taken from inaccessible full text.
Supports PCL biodegradability under stated assay conditions, not the claim that the present article will rapidly and fully biodegrade at home.

sources.title: Enhanced Marine Biodegradation of Polycaprolactone through Incorporation of Mucus Bubble Powder from Violet Sea Snail as Protein Fillers
verified_factual_subset: Pure PCL and 95/5 PCL/marine protein filler sheets were studied; the PCL material was reported as number-average molecular weight 8000.
Sample preparation used tetrahydrofuran solution casting and cryomilling before 70-degree-Celsius, 10-MPa pressing; this is outside the proposed home protocol.
BOD tests used sediment-enriched extracted seawater at 20 degrees Celsius for 56 days with added nitrogen/phosphorus nutrients.
The paper reports maximum BOD biodegradation approximately 55% for pure PCL and 96% for the 5% protein-filled PCL; corresponding endpoint sheet mass losses were about 33.4% and 34.1%.
The reported initial pure-PCL water contact angle was 94.3 degrees.
transfer_limits: BOD, mass loss and contact angle are distinct endpoints and must not be substituted for one another.
Enriched/nutrient-supplemented seawater, low-molecular-weight PCL and thin pressed sheets do not establish home-compost behavior or thick craft-part fate.
Contact angle does not prove leak-free containment or resistance to continuous immersion.
The marine-protein formulation and organic-solvent processing are not recommended for home reproduction.

sources.title: Alginate-Based Edible Films and Coatings for Food Packaging Applications
sources.evidence_level: review; accessible full text; source comparison rather than direct experiment
verified_factual_subset: Alginate film crosslinking uses divalent calcium ions, and the review discusses calcium chloride, calcium lactate and calcium gluconate as different calcium sources.
The review reports source-dependent solubility and gelation kinetics; calcium lactate and gluconate are alternatives where taste is important.
The review discusses the plasticization/water-barrier tradeoff: glycerol can improve flexibility while increasing water-vapor permeability.
transfer_limits: Review statements do not validate the present alginate/glycerol/calcium-lactate/beeswax recipe.
Calcium salts differ in formula mass, hydration state and calcium fraction; equal gram doses are not equivalent calcium-ion doses.
An ionically crosslinked alginate network may remain intact yet absorb and swell in water; that is not waterproof performance.
Ingredient biodegradability and edible-coating use do not certify the fabricated article as home-compostable or suitable for food contact.

sources.title: A Novel Sodium Alginate-Carnauba Wax Film Containing Calcium Ascorbate: Structural Properties and Preservative Effect on Fresh-Cut Apples
verified_factual_subset: Methods report 1 g sodium alginate in 100 mL water, 0.3 g carnauba wax, 0.2 mL glycerol and 0.4 g calcium ascorbate; the casting solution was dried at 50 degrees Celsius.
Water-vapor testing used calcium-chloride-filled cups at 25 degrees Celsius and 75% relative humidity over two days.
The water-solubility method exposed film to 20 mL distilled water for 24 hours and recovered/dried insoluble material.
The authors report a 31% decrease in film water solubility with 0.3% carnauba wax, rather than zero solubility; wax without glycerol introduced brittleness and cracks.
transfer_limits: This formulation uses calcium ascorbate and dispersed carnauba wax, not a calcium-lactate-crosslinked film with a surface beeswax coating.
The source does not give a numerical processing temperature for wax dispersion; 50 degrees Celsius is the drying temperature.
Solubility reduction, water-vapor barrier and apple preservation do not demonstrate long-term waterproof containment.
Temperature, drying and solvent-free ingredient similarity do not validate a new recipe or establish food-contact safety.

sources.title: Preparation of Novel Flaxseed Oil/Beeswax Oleogel Systems and Its Application in the Improvement of Sodium Alginate Films
verified_factual_subset: Beeswax/flaxseed-oil oleogel was prepared in an 80-degree-Celsius water bath for 20 minutes.

Film preparation used 1.5% sodium alginate, hydrated at 80 degrees Celsius for 30 minutes; oleogel was stirred into the aqueous phase at 60 degrees Celsius, with ultrasonic degassing and 30-degree-Celsius drying for 24 hours.
The optimized film reported tensile strength 25.11 +/- 1.24 MPa, elongation 58.21 +/- 1.58%, and water-vapor permeability (0.82 +/- 0.04) x 10^-5 g cm/(cm2 kPa h).
transfer_limits: Beeswax/oil oleogel dispersion is not the proposed calcium-crosslinked alginate core plus pure-beeswax surface layer.
The methods state glycerol percentages with an ambiguous film-weight basis; they should not be silently converted into a precise home formula.
No retrieved water-immersion leakage test or environmental mineralization/compost certification validates this film.
Analytical organic reagents listed elsewhere in the paper are not needed or recommended for the proposed home preparation.

sources.title: Development and Characterization of Calcium Lactate-Activated Sodium Alginate-Gum Arabic Edible Films
sources.evidence_level: primary research; accessible publisher PDF; protocol inconsistencies noted
verified_factual_subset: The methods report a 2.87% w/v calcium-lactate spray applied at five positions about 20 cm from cast alginate/gum-arabic films.
Alginate/gum-arabic dissolution used 80 degrees Celsius for 15 minutes; drying used 35 degrees Celsius for 24 hours.
Reported WVTR values span 69–94 g/(m2 day), measured over 24 hours at approximately 55% relative humidity.
transfer_limits: The paper does not specify calcium-lactate hydrate form or spray volume; the calcium dose is not reproducible from concentration alone.
The formulation table and methods differ in glycerol/peppermint-oil quantities, and abstract/table tensile-strength assignments differ.
The peppermint-oil/gum-arabic/spray formulation is not the proposed alginate/glycerol/beeswax film with a lactate immersion bath.
WVTR is a vapor transport endpoint, not a continuous-immersion or leak test; no measured biodegradation assay is supplied.

sources.title: Scalable production of hydrophobic starch/beeswax films by continuous solution casting
verified_factual_subset: The deposited abstract reports surfactant-free starch/beeswax films made by pilot-scale continuous solution casting.
The study explored beeswax/starch mass ratios 0.3–0.7 and reports contact-angle and water-vapor permeability improvements.
transfer_limits: No exact home mixing temperature, immersion swelling, leakage or mineralization results were verified from full text.
Contact-angle and WVP improvements alone do not demonstrate waterproofness.
This establishes starch/wax prior art, not the novelty or performance of the present candidate.

sources.title: Ingevity: Bioplastics and Capa thermoplastic certification claims
sources.evidence_level: manufacturer product information; not independent performance validation
verified_factual_subset: The manufacturer lists OK compost HOME, OK compost INDUSTRIAL, OK biodegradable SOIL, MARINE and WATER among certifications for its Capa portfolio.
It identifies Capa 6250, 6400, 6500, 6500D and 6800 among offered thermoplastic grades.
transfer_limits: The retrieved portfolio page does not supply independently checked certificate identifiers, covered geometries, thickness limits or test reports.
A claim for specified commercial grades must not be transferred to an unspecified craft grade or to a novel native-starch-filled article.
No arbitrary home-compost schedule, landfill behavior or permission to discard plastics into water follows from a portfolio claim.
